source.title: Understanding Task Representations in Neural Networks via Bayesian Ablation
source.authors: Andrew Nam; Declan Campbell; Thomas L. Griffiths; Jonathan D. Cohen; Sarah-Jane Leslie

record.file_problem: No apparent text problem; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies task information and polysemanticity in a small semantic-cognition model, but does not test any listed version about neuron-job audits, explanation prediction, or automated explanation scores.
record.gate_note: The paper reports measurements of task information in individual units and ensembles. These are related to neuron specialization but do not measure the job-count shares or explanation performance named in the claim versions; the rows are recorded as findings that fit no version.
record.test_reason: The study introduces Bayesian ablation mask distributions and applies them to the 24-unit task layer of a small ISC semantic-cognition network. It measures how much task information single units carry. It audits no language-model neuron poles and scores no natural-language explanations. It does not build attribution graphs or study InceptionV1. No version is tested. The per-unit task-information result concerns a related construct (task polysemanticity in a toy multitask net), so it goes under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors present ablation mask distributions as a causal, information-theoretic framework for task representations. In the ISC model, task representations are predominantly modular (entropy drop of 4.62%). Single units carry little task information while ensembles carry much, which implies structured polysemanticity. They acknowledge validation on only one model and dataset, and that the GFlowNet approximation is hard to scale.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Bayesian ablation-mask distributions and information-theoretic measures on a small semantic-cognition model; it does not audit neuron poles or test natural-language explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that using odds ratios rather than raw accuracy changes alignment with other representational measures and task-acquisition order.

fits_no_version.finding: In the ISC task layer, single units reduce task uncertainty by about 4.21% in most cases. The authors read this as units contributing to multiple tasks in a structured (polysemantic) way.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a small multitask feed-forward network, individual task-layer units carry little task-specific causal information alone and participate in multiple tasks.

fits_no_version.finding: Full ablation masks reduce task uncertainty by 82.6% on average, far more than single units. This indicates distributed, ensemble task coding.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a small multitask network, task identity is causally encoded by ensembles of units rather than by single units.

record.peer_reviewed: Proceedings of Machine Learning Research 323; 5th Conference on Causal Learning and Reasoning
record.problems: Empirical validation focuses on one dataset and the ISC model. The authors also state that the abstract measures require further validation and that scaling the approximation to more ablatable units is challenging.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported analyses, including task similarity, task differentiation, and GFlowNet approximation accuracy, do not measure unit job specificity or explanation performance and were left out.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B audit and no shares of poles by job count.
No language models, dense or mixture-of-experts, at any scale.
No InceptionV1, cat/car neuron, pose, or recursive-generalization analysis.
No comparison of architecture, regularization or tools against interpretable-neuron share.
No attribution graphs and no test of neurons as circuit units against replacement models.
No natural-language explanations from activating examples tested for prediction.

record.verdict_notes: Single ISC model (10 seeds), 24-unit task layer, sigmoid units. 'Polysemanticity' here means a unit's spread across 36 tasks, not across features or concepts. The authors note that low task specificity may coexist with meaningful sub-task structure. This makes the result even less comparable to the neuron-pole job-share claims.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B or report the shares of poles with one job, two related jobs, or not-yet-understood jobs.
Uses an ISC semantic-cognition network, not language models across sizes or dense and mixture-of-experts architectures.
Does not study InceptionV1 or cat-and-car features, pose, recursive generalization, or superposition.
Does not compare architecture, regularization, or tool effects on interpretability shares, or provide the InceptionV1-sized estimates.
Does not build attribution graphs or assess whether neurons suffice as circuit units.
Does not test whether explanations based on activating examples predict where units fire.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: It discusses unit polysemanticity with respect to tasks, citing Elhage 2022 and Bricken 2023, in its own setting. It does not test or use the claim.

tranche.reason: The study uses a small ISC semantic-cognition MLP with a 24-unit task layer. It does not audit language-model neuron poles, score explanations, revisit InceptionV1 or build attribution graphs, so no version is tested.

source_check.notes: Both values match the text: about 4.21% NMI for single units 'in most cases', and an 82.6% average for full masks, over 10 ISC instances, a 24-unit task layer and 36 tasks. The authors note that low task-NMI units may still encode sub-task structure, so this is not a measure of neuron interpretability. Bears on no version V1-V7.
